analogy.p: Think of the atmosphere as a duvet on a bed. Your body (the Earth's surface) gives out heat all the time, and the duvet (greenhouse gases) slows how fast it escapes, so you stay warm. A thin duvet is perfect; but if you keep adding duvets (more carbon dioxide and methane) you overheat. Deforestation is like removing the fan that was cooling the room (trees that absorb carbon dioxide) while also burning the furniture for heat. Where it breaks down: a duvet traps heat by blocking air movement, whereas greenhouse gases work by absorbing and re-radiating infrared radiation.
analogy.t: A greenhouse blanket on a cold night

bullets: **Global warming** = the gradual increase in the average temperature of the Earth's surface and atmosphere, linked to rising levels of greenhouse gases.
The two greenhouse gases named in the specification are **carbon dioxide (CO2)** and **methane (CH4)**.
You need to describe **biological consequences** of global warming, not just say 'it gets hotter'. Think habitats, distribution, migration, breeding and food chains.
**Deforestation** = the permanent clearing of forests (large-scale removal of trees), especially tropical rainforest, so that the land can be used for something else.
Peat bogs are a store of carbon; destroying them releases CO2 and removes habitats.
Command words: **describe** (say what happens), **explain** (say what happens AND why), **evaluate** (weigh up both sides and reach a judgement).
This topic links forwards to **maintaining biodiversity** (programmes to reduce these harms) and backwards to the **carbon cycle**.
core.h: 1. What the specification wants you to know
core.p: This topic sits in AQA 4.7 Ecology (Paper 2) under 'Biodiversity and the effect of human activity on ecosystems'. You must be able to explain how **carbon dioxide and methane are greenhouse gases**, how increasing amounts of them contribute to **global warming**, and describe the **biological consequences** of global warming. You must also explain how **large-scale deforestation** and the **destruction of peat bogs** damage ecosystems and make global warming worse. Examiners love this topic because it joins up several ideas from the whole course: photosynthesis, respiration, decay, the carbon cycle, food chains, competition and biodiversity.

bullets: The Sun's energy arrives as short-wave radiation which passes mostly straight through the atmosphere (figure 1).
The Earth's surface absorbs it and re-emits it as **longer wavelength infrared radiation**.
Greenhouse gases (carbon dioxide, methane, water vapour) **absorb** infrared and **re-radiate** it, some of it back towards the surface. This is why the effect is described as a 'blanket'.
The natural greenhouse effect is **beneficial**: it keeps the average surface temperature at a level suitable for liquid water and life.
The problem is the **enhanced greenhouse effect**: human activities have increased the concentration of greenhouse gases so more infrared is trapped and the average temperature rises.

Energy balance idea (Higher thinking): a stable temperature needs energy in = energy out. More greenhouse gases reduce the energy escaping, so the surface warms until the outgoing energy rises again to match the incoming.
Do not confuse this with the **ozone layer** (which absorbs ultraviolet and is a separate issue) or with 'acid rain' (caused by sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides). These are common exam mix-ups.
core.h: 2. The greenhouse effect: a natural and necessary process
core.p: The **greenhouse effect** is a natural process that keeps the Earth warm enough for life. Energy reaches the Earth from the Sun mainly as short-wave radiation (visible light and some ultraviolet). Some is reflected back into space by clouds and light surfaces such as ice, and the rest is absorbed by the land and oceans, which warms them. The warm surface then gives out energy as infrared (thermal) radiation. **Greenhouse gases** in the atmosphere absorb some of this outgoing infrared radiation and re-radiate it in all directions, including back down to the surface, so less energy escapes to space and the lower atmosphere stays warmer. Without any greenhouse effect the Earth would be so cold that most life could not survive.

bullets: **Burning fossil fuels** (coal, oil, natural gas) in power stations, vehicles and homes is the biggest source: combustion of hydrocarbons produces carbon dioxide and water.
**Deforestation**: trees are cut and burnt or left to rot, releasing the carbon they stored, and fewer trees remain to take carbon dioxide out of the air by photosynthesis.
**Respiration** by all living organisms and **decay** by microorganisms release carbon dioxide too, but in a natural balanced cycle these are matched by photosynthesis.
The key idea is an **imbalance**: more carbon dioxide is being added to the atmosphere than is being removed, so the concentration rises.
Carbon dioxide stays in the atmosphere for a very long time, so the effect of today's emissions lasts for decades to centuries.

**Graph skill**: in figure 3 the line is almost flat until about 1850 then gets steeper. Describe it as 'rises slowly then increasingly rapidly from about 1900, from about 280 ppm to over 400 ppm'. Quote values with units.

Rising carbon dioxide levels match rising average temperatures. This is a **correlation**. Scientists accept a causal link because there is a well-understood mechanism (the greenhouse effect), not because of the graph alone.
core.h: 3. Carbon dioxide: sources and why it is rising
core.p: Carbon dioxide makes up only a tiny fraction of the atmosphere (around 0.04 percent, about 420 parts per million today) but small changes have a large effect on heat trapping. Before the Industrial Revolution the concentration was about 280 ppm and it has risen steeply since, as shown in figure 3. The extra carbon dioxide comes mostly from human activities that move carbon that was locked away for millions of years (in coal, oil and gas) into the atmosphere, and from the loss of forests that would otherwise absorb it.

bullets: **Cattle and other ruminants**: microorganisms in the digestive system produce methane that is released mainly by belching.
**Rice paddy fields**: the flooded soil is low in oxygen, so microorganisms decomposing plant material there release methane (**anaerobic decay**).
**Landfill sites** and rotting waste produce methane because buried waste decays without much oxygen. This is why recycling and composting help (see the maintaining biodiversity note).
Methane is also released during the extraction of natural gas and coal, and from wetlands (a natural source).
Rising populations eat more meat and rice, so demand for cattle and rice land rises. This is the link between food, deforestation and methane.
Methane has a shorter life in the air than carbon dioxide but traps more heat per molecule, so reducing methane emissions can slow warming relatively quickly.
Exam tip: if asked how farming increases greenhouse gases, give **both** gases and the source for each: cattle and rice paddies for methane; clearing and burning forest for carbon dioxide.
core.h: 4. Methane: sources and why it matters
core.p: Methane is a hydrocarbon gas (CH4). There is much less of it in the atmosphere than carbon dioxide, but each molecule traps far more heat, so it is a powerful greenhouse gas. The specification links methane to two farming activities that increase with deforestation: keeping large numbers of **cattle** and growing **rice in paddy fields**. In both cases microorganisms release methane when they break down material in places where there is little or no oxygen.

bullets: Evidence includes **records of average global temperature**, atmospheric carbon dioxide measurements, shrinking glaciers and sea ice, and rising sea level.
Measurements are made by many independent groups, using many methods, which makes the conclusions more **reliable** and **valid**.
Models predict future change but contain **uncertainty** because the climate is so complex. This is why predictions are often given as ranges.
A good scientific answer separates **evidence** (data collected) from **prediction** (what models suggest) and from **opinion**.
Sea level rises for two main reasons: **melting of ice on land** (glaciers and ice sheets) and **thermal expansion** of warmer sea water. Melting floating sea ice does not by itself raise sea level.
Some regions warm faster than others, and warming is not the same as 'hotter every single day': it is a long-term average.
Politicians and scientists weigh up the benefits of using fossil fuels (cheap energy, jobs) against the long-term harm, which is why global agreements are difficult.
core.h: 5. Global warming: what it is and the evidence
core.p: **Global warming** is the rise in the average temperature of the Earth's atmosphere and oceans caused (in large part) by an enhanced greenhouse effect. Most climate scientists agree that human activity is the main cause of the warming observed since the 1900s. The consequences are often called **climate change**, because warming also changes rainfall patterns, ice cover and the frequency of extreme weather. As scientists gather data from many places and many years, the evidence becomes more reliable.

bullets: Habitat = the place where an organism lives. When it is flooded with sea water, freshwater and land species may not tolerate the **salt** and may die.
Species that cannot move quickly (plants, small invertebrates) are the most at risk of local extinction.
Coastal habitats such as **mangroves, salt marshes and coral reefs** are particularly affected by rising sea level and warming water.
Smaller habitat = fewer resources (food, shelter, nesting sites) = **intense competition** = smaller populations that may be wiped out by disease or chance events.
Human populations are affected too: farmland, homes and freshwater sources near the coast may be lost.
Link to **biodiversity**: fewer habitats means fewer niches, so fewer species can live in the area.
Exam model phrase: 'sea level rises, low-lying areas flooded, **habitats are lost**, so populations of species fall / species may become extinct.'
core.h: 6. Biological consequence 1: loss of habitat from flooding
core.p: As global temperatures rise, ice stored on land melts and the oceans expand, so **sea level rises**. Low-lying coastal land such as river deltas, salt marshes, mudflats and islands can be flooded by the sea. This causes **loss of habitat** for the plants and animals that live there, and as habitats shrink the populations they support fall, so biodiversity can fall as well.

bullets: **Distribution** = where a species is found. Warm-adapted species spread into new areas, while cold-adapted species lose their range and may have nowhere cooler to go.
Mountain and Arctic species are at particular risk as their cool habitat shrinks.
Migrating animals (for example some birds) may arrive earlier, take different routes or no longer migrate as far.
New species moving in may **compete** with, or prey on, native species, or bring in new diseases and pests.
If one species moves but another that depends on it does not, **food chains and relationships** are broken.
Changes in rainfall as well as temperature alter which plants can grow, which then affects the animals that feed on them.
In an exam, link cause and effect: 'temperature rises so conditions are no longer suitable, so species **move to cooler areas**, changing distribution'.
core.h: 7. Biological consequence 2: changes in distribution and migration
core.p: Every species is adapted to a particular range of **abiotic conditions**, such as temperature and rainfall. As the climate warms, the places that suit a species change. Species may **change their distribution**, which means moving to new areas, usually towards the poles or up mountains where it is cooler. The timing and routes of **migration** can also change, because migrating animals respond to temperature and food supply. Species that cannot move or adapt fast enough decline.

bullets: **Breeding patterns** may change: earlier spring means earlier breeding, or in some species longer breeding seasons.
A **mismatch** between predator and prey timings reduces food available for offspring, so fewer survive and the population falls.
Food chains are interdependent: loss or movement of a producer affects primary consumers, which then affects secondary consumers and so on.
Some species may benefit from warmer conditions (more growth, longer growing season), so global warming creates winners and losers.
Overall effect: a change in the **community**, usually a loss of biodiversity as specialists decline and generalists spread.
Link: **interdependence** is the idea that species in a community depend on each other for food, shelter, pollination and seed dispersal.
Exam tip: pick consequences from the spec list (habitat loss, distribution/migration, breeding and food chains) and always explain the link in one chain of reasoning.
core.h: 8. Biological consequence 3: breeding cycles and food chains
core.p: Many organisms time key events, such as flowering, egg laying and hatching, using temperature and day length. Warming can shift these events earlier in the year. Different species may respond by different amounts, which can cause a **mismatch** in a food chain. For example, if insects that young birds feed on appear earlier in spring but the birds hatch at their old time, the chicks may starve. Changes like this show how a change in one factor passes along the food web.

bullets: **Cattle ranching**: forest is cleared to make grazing land and to grow animal feed.
**Rice fields**: flooded paddy fields produce methane, as explained earlier.

**Biofuels**: crops (such as sugar cane, palm oil or maize) are grown to produce fuels such as ethanol and biodiesel. These are intended to reduce carbon dioxide from fossil fuels, but clearing forest to grow them can release more carbon than is saved.
**Timber and paper** are harvested for sale.
**Population and economic pressure**: people in poorer countries may clear land to grow food and earn income, so this is a social and economic issue, not just a biological one.
**Evaluation point**: developing countries may argue it is unfair to ask them not to use their land when richer countries industrialised using fossil fuels.
Scientists, governments and conservation groups work to slow deforestation (see maintaining biodiversity).
core.h: 9. Deforestation: what it is and why it happens
core.p: **Deforestation** is the large-scale clearing of forests. In tropical regions it has been carried out to provide land for **cattle and rice fields** (which increase methane), and to grow crops from which **biofuels** can be produced. Other reasons include timber for sale, building roads and settlements, and mining. Tropical rainforests contain huge numbers of species, so clearing them is a major threat to biodiversity, and the trees store huge amounts of carbon.

bullets: **Burning** the trees (slash and burn) releases the stored carbon as carbon dioxide by combustion.
**Decay**: felled wood left to rot is broken down by microorganisms, which respire and release carbon dioxide.
**Fewer trees** means **less photosynthesis**, so less carbon dioxide is removed from the atmosphere.
Machinery and transport used in clearing and moving logs burn fossil fuels, adding carbon dioxide.
Replacing forest with **cattle** and **rice fields** adds methane as well as removing a carbon store.
Deforested soil can lose carbon as it is exposed and eroded.
Net effect: the carbon cycle becomes **unbalanced**; more carbon dioxide is added to the atmosphere than is removed, so the greenhouse effect is enhanced.

Model sentence: 'Trees absorb carbon dioxide by photosynthesis. When they are cut down and burnt or decay, this carbon dioxide is released, and fewer trees remain to absorb it, so atmospheric carbon dioxide increases.'
core.h: 10. How deforestation increases carbon dioxide in the atmosphere
core.p: Forests are major carbon stores and carbon sinks. Living trees take carbon dioxide from the air during **photosynthesis** and build it into sugars, cellulose and wood. When forest is cleared, carbon dioxide levels in the atmosphere rise through several separate routes at the same time (figure 2). Examiners usually want you to give at least two distinct routes, and to explain the reasoning, in a typical 4 mark question.

bullets: **Loss of habitat** and food sources, leading to local extinctions and reduced **biodiversity**. Many tropical species live in a very small area and have nowhere else to go.
**Soil erosion**: roots no longer hold soil together, so rain washes the topsoil away. Rivers become silted and fertile soil is lost.
**Leaching of nutrients**: heavy rain washes minerals from bare soil. Fertility drops quickly after clearing because most nutrients are held in the living plants, not the soil.
**Water cycle changes**: fewer trees means less transpiration, so less water vapour returns to the air, and rainfall may fall locally, making the region drier.
**Food chains** are broken because producers are removed, and the species that depend on them (and on one another) decline.
The loss of species may remove organisms with potential uses, such as unknown medicines or food crops.
Once a rainforest is cleared, it may take hundreds of years to recover, or may never recover, so effects are long-lasting.
core.h: 11. Other effects of deforestation on ecosystems
core.p: Carbon dioxide is only part of the story. Forest trees provide habitats, food and shelter for thousands of species, so removing them has a direct effect on biodiversity. Removing trees also changes the physical environment: soil, water and local climate. These effects are linked, so you can chain them together to produce high-mark explanations.

bullets: Peat forms because **waterlogged, acidic, low-oxygen conditions slow down decay** by microorganisms.
Digging up peat exposes it to **oxygen**, so decomposers respire and release carbon dioxide. Burning peat releases it by combustion.
Peat bogs are **habitats** for specialist plants and animals, so removing them reduces biodiversity.
Peat takes thousands of years to form, so it is effectively a **non-renewable** resource when used for compost.
Alternatives include peat-free compost made from composted garden waste, bark or coir, which also reduces landfill.
Link to the carbon cycle: a carbon store (peat) is turned into an atmospheric carbon dioxide source in a short time.
Evaluation: gardeners and growers like peat compost because it is cheap, light and holds water, which is why change needs regulation and public awareness.
core.h: 12. Peat bogs: destroying a carbon store
core.p: **Peat** is partly decayed plant material that builds up very slowly in waterlogged soil where there is little oxygen, so decay is incomplete. Over thousands of years, large amounts of carbon are stored in peat. The specification states that peat bogs have been destroyed to produce **garden compost**. When peat is dug up and dried, or burnt, the stored carbon is released as **carbon dioxide** as microorganisms decay it in the air, so the peat bog changes from a carbon store into a carbon source.

bullets: **Describe a trend**: say what happens, quote start and end values with units, and mention any change in rate (for example 'slowly at first, then more steeply').
**Percentage change** = (new value minus original value) divided by original value, times 100.
**Rate of change** = change in quantity divided by time taken (for example ppm per year or hectares per year).
**Correlation does not prove causation**: two things rising together might both be caused by something else. Strong evidence needs a mechanism and repeatable data.
**Reliability**: data from many independent sources, repeated over many years, is more reliable than a single study.
**Bias**: a source with a vested interest (such as a company selling a product) may present data selectively.
**Evaluate** means a balanced answer: advantages, disadvantages, then a clear conclusion that uses the evidence given.
Check the **axes**: some graphs do not start at zero, which can exaggerate changes.
core.p: Exam questions often give a graph or table of carbon dioxide levels, temperatures or forest area and ask you to describe a trend, calculate a change, or suggest a conclusion. Others give a scenario and ask you to evaluate. A good approach is to use the data first, then add the biology. Always use numbers with units, and be careful about claiming that one thing definitely causes another.

bullets: **Carbon cycle link**: photosynthesis removes carbon dioxide, while respiration, combustion and decay add it. Deforestation shifts the balance.
**Biodiversity link**: fewer species make ecosystems less stable and less able to cope with further change.
**Food security link**: changing climate affects crop yields and farming areas.
**Waste link**: rotting waste in landfill produces methane, so waste management is also a global warming issue.
**Solutions** (see maintaining biodiversity): reduce deforestation, replant forests, cut fossil fuel use, reduce methane, restore peat bogs, use peat-free compost.
**Ethical and economic issues**: poorer countries may depend on forest land for income, so solutions need international cooperation and fairness.
**Time scale issue**: effects continue long after emissions are cut because carbon dioxide stays in the atmosphere, so action is urgent.
core.h: 14. Linking ideas: the big picture and Higher-tier thinking
core.p: The best answers link several ideas in a clear chain. For example: deforestation leads to less photosynthesis and more burning and decay, so carbon dioxide rises; this enhances the greenhouse effect; warming raises sea level and shifts climate zones; habitats are lost and species move or die; biodiversity falls and food chains collapse. Each arrow in that chain is a mark. Being able to move between the carbon cycle, ecology and human impact is what separates grade 9 answers from grade 6 answers.

exam: **Describe** (2 to 3 marks): state what happens using precise terms: 'carbon dioxide levels increased from about 280 ppm to over 400 ppm'. Always quote data with units.

**Explain** (typically 3 to 4 marks): give a cause and a reason for each mark. Use 'because', 'so', 'which leads to'. Chain: more greenhouse gases, more infrared absorbed and re-radiated, temperature rises.
**1 mark**: name the gases: carbon dioxide and methane. Know one source for each: burning fossil fuels or deforestation for carbon dioxide; cattle or rice fields for methane.
**Deforestation 4 marker**: give at least two routes for more carbon dioxide (burning, decay by microorganisms, less photosynthesis) and a link to the greenhouse effect.

**Biological consequences**: choose from loss of habitat from flooding of low-lying areas, changes in distribution and migration, and changes to breeding and food chains. Explain each in one linked sentence.

**6 mark 'evaluate'**: give benefits of the action (for example growing biofuels or clearing land for cattle), then the drawbacks, then a justified conclusion using evidence from the question. Use a clear structure: for, against, conclusion.
**Graphs**: read values accurately, comment on rate of change, include units and the time period. Do not claim causation from correlation alone.
**Calculations**: write the formula, substitute, give the answer with units and a sensible number of significant figures. Percentage change = change divided by original times 100.
**Link marks**: examiners reward words that show reasoning: 'therefore', 'as a result', 'this means'. Avoid vague words like 'bad for the environment'; say exactly what is damaged.
**Use key terms**: greenhouse gases, absorb, infrared, re-radiate, photosynthesis, combustion, decay, biodiversity, habitat. Marks are often lost for everyday wording.

mistakes.r: Greenhouse gases absorb infrared radiation and re-radiate it. The ozone layer absorbs ultraviolet and is a separate issue.
mistakes.w: The greenhouse effect is caused by holes in the ozone layer.

mistakes.r: Greenhouse gases absorb infrared radiation from the Earth's surface and re-radiate it, so less energy escapes to space.
mistakes.w: Global warming happens because carbon dioxide traps heat like a lid / the Sun gets hotter.

mistakes.r: Deforestation increases atmospheric carbon dioxide (burning, decay, less photosynthesis) and reduces habitats and biodiversity.
mistakes.w: Deforestation just means there are fewer trees, so less oxygen.

mistakes.r: Methane comes from cattle and rice paddy fields (microorganisms in low oxygen), and from decaying waste.
mistakes.w: Methane comes from burning fossil fuels only.

mistakes.r: Living trees absorb more carbon dioxide in photosynthesis than they release; cutting them down removes this removal and releases stored carbon.
mistakes.w: Trees release carbon dioxide so deforestation reduces it.

mistakes.r: Sea level rises due to melting land ice and thermal expansion of warmer water; melting floating ice has little effect.
mistakes.w: Sea level rises because ice cubes melt in the sea.

mistakes.r: Give specific consequences: habitat loss from flooding, changes to distribution and migration, breeding and food chains disrupted.
mistakes.w: Animals just die because it gets too hot.

mistakes.r: Peat is a carbon store; exposing it to oxygen causes decay and releases carbon dioxide, and bogs are habitats.
mistakes.w: Peat is just soil, so digging it up is harmless.

mistakes.r: Biofuels can reduce fossil fuel use, but clearing forest to grow them releases carbon dioxide and destroys habitats.
mistakes.w: Biofuels are always good because they are not fossil fuels.

summary: The specification asks you to explain how carbon dioxide and methane act as greenhouse gases, how rising levels cause global warming, and to describe its biological consequences (habitat loss from flooding, changes to distribution and migration, and disruption of breeding and food chains). You must also explain how large-scale deforestation and the destruction of peat bogs release carbon dioxide and reduce biodiversity. It matters because it links the carbon cycle, ecosystems and human impact, and it is a regular source of 4 and 6 mark questions on Paper 2.

terms.d: A gas in the atmosphere, such as carbon dioxide or methane, that absorbs infrared radiation from the Earth's surface and re-radiates it, helping to keep the Earth warm.
The natural process by which greenhouse gases trap energy in the atmosphere and keep the Earth's surface warmer than it would otherwise be.
The increase in the average temperature of the Earth's surface and atmosphere, caused largely by increasing amounts of greenhouse gases from human activity.
Long-term changes in weather patterns, including temperature, rainfall and sea level, resulting from global warming.
A greenhouse gas (CO2) released by respiration, combustion and decay and removed from the air by photosynthesis.
A greenhouse gas (CH4) produced by cattle and by rice paddy fields (and decaying waste) where microorganisms break down material without much oxygen.
The large-scale clearing or removal of forests, for example to provide land for cattle and rice fields or to grow crops for biofuels.
A fuel made from plant material, such as ethanol or biodiesel, grown to replace fossil fuels.
Partly decayed plant material that builds up in waterlogged, low-oxygen conditions; it stores large amounts of carbon.
A part of the environment, such as forest or peat, that absorbs and holds carbon, removing carbon dioxide from the atmosphere.
The variety of all the different species of organisms on Earth, or within an ecosystem.
The place where an organism lives.
Where in the world, or in an area, a species is found.
The regular movement of animals from one area to another, usually in response to seasonal changes in temperature or food.
When there are no living individuals of a species left.
Microorganisms (bacteria and fungi) that break down dead material and release carbon dioxide through respiration.
Burning, which releases the carbon stored in fuels or wood as carbon dioxide.
A unit used to measure the concentration of a gas in the atmosphere.

worked.q: The concentration of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere was about 280 ppm in 1750 and about 420 ppm in 2023. Calculate the percentage increase. (2 marks)

A tropical forest covers 8000 km2. It is cleared at 240 km2 per year. (a) Calculate the percentage of the forest cleared each year. (b) Estimate how many years it would take to clear all the forest at this rate. (3 marks)
steps: = 33.3... so about 33 years (to the nearest whole year; the forest would be gone in just over 33 years)
Note: the rate may change over time, so this is only an estimate.

worked.ans: Model answer: Trees absorb carbon dioxide during photosynthesis, so removing them means less is removed from the atmosphere. Burning the trees and the decay of dead wood by microorganisms release carbon dioxide. Cleared land is often used for cattle and rice fields, which release methane. Carbon dioxide and methane are greenhouse gases which absorb infrared radiation and re-radiate it, so the greenhouse effect is enhanced and global warming increases.
worked.q: Explain how large-scale deforestation can increase global warming. (4 marks)
steps: Mark 1: trees take in carbon dioxide from the air by photosynthesis, so fewer trees means less carbon dioxide is removed.
Mark 2: when the trees are burnt, carbon dioxide is released by combustion.
Mark 3: when the wood decays, microorganisms respire and release carbon dioxide (cattle and rice fields on cleared land also release methane).
Mark 4: carbon dioxide and methane are greenhouse gases that absorb infrared radiation and re-radiate it, so more heat is trapped and the average temperature of the Earth rises.
